hello.title: Hello, R
hello.summary: Write your first R code: print values, show text with cat() and calculate with numbers.
hello.lesson.0: R is a programming language for data and statistics. A program is a list of instructions that R runs from top to bottom. The function `print()` shows a value on the screen. Text goes in double quotes: `"Hello, R!"` is a **string**.
hello.lesson.2: The `[1]` at the start of the line is the position of the first value on that line. In R, even a single value is stored as a **vector**, a sequence of values, here with only one element. You learn more about vectors in unit 3. `print()` also shows strings with their quotes.
hello.lesson.5: The function `cat()` writes text as it is, without `[1]` and without quotes. It does not end the line by itself, so you add `"\n"`, the **newline** character, at the end. When you give `cat()` several values, separated by commas, it puts a space between them.
hello.lesson.8: R can calculate. `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies, `/` divides and `^` raises to a power. `%%` gives the remainder of a division, and `%/%` divides and drops the remainder. As in mathematics, `^` comes first, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`. Parentheses change the order.
hello.lesson.10: A **comment** starts with `#`. R ignores everything from `#` to the end of the line. In this course, comments only show results, like `# 6` below.
hello.lesson.12: R is case-sensitive: `print` and `Print` are different names. `Print("Hi")` stops with the error `could not find function "Print"`.
hello.card.1: `cat("Hi\n")` writes text without quotes; `"\n"` ends the line
hello-1.explain: `*` comes before `-`: `4 * 2` is 8, and `10 - 8` is 2. `print()` puts `[1]` in front.
hello-2.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2. `cat()` writes both values with a space between them.
hello-3.prompt: Which line writes Hello without quotes and without `[1]`?
hello-3.explain: `cat()` writes text as it is. `print()` adds `[1]` and quotes, `Print` does not exist, and `Hello` without quotes is not a string.
hello-5.explain: `%/%` drops the remainder, so the result is `3`. `7 / 2` would give `3.5`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the remainder of 10 divided by 3.
hello-6.explain: `%%` gives the remainder: 10 is 3 times 3 plus 1.
hello-7.prompt: Complete the code so the line ends after the text.
hello-7.explain: The newline character is written `"\n"`, with a backslash.
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that writes Hello R and ends the line.
hello-8.explain: `cat()` writes both strings with a space between them, and `"\n"` ends the line.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Start, then `[1] 6`, then End.
hello-9.explain: R runs the lines from top to bottom, so the order of the lines is the order of the output.
hello-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-10.pairs.0: shows a value with its position
hello-11.explain: R is case-sensitive. The function is called `print`, with a small `p`.
hello-12.explain: The string has no closing quote. Write `print("Hello")`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables, get to know numeric, character and logical values, and join text with paste().
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name that stores a value. In R you create one with `<-`, the assignment arrow: a less-than sign followed by a minus. Read `age <- 30` as "age gets 30". You can give a variable a new value later, even one that uses its old value.
variables.lesson.2: A name can contain letters, digits, `.` and `_`, and it starts with a letter: `price`, `total_2`, `first.name`. Names are case-sensitive, so `age` and `Age` are two different variables. `=` also works for assignment, but most R code uses `<-`.
variables.lesson.4: Every value has a type. Numbers are `numeric`, text in quotes is `character`, and the two values `TRUE` and `FALSE` are `logical`. The function `class()` tells you the type of a value.
variables.lesson.6: Whole numbers are `numeric` too. If you need a real whole-number type, add `L` after the number: `5L` is an `integer`. Most of the time, `numeric` is all you need.
variables.lesson.9: `paste()` joins values into one string and puts a space between them. `paste0()` joins them without a space. Numbers are turned into text automatically.
variables.lesson.11: `nchar()` counts the characters of a string, and `toupper()` writes it in capital letters. `as.numeric()` turns text like `"2.5"` into a number, and `as.character()` turns a number into text.
variables.lesson.13: You cannot calculate with text. `"5" + 1` stops with the error `non-numeric argument to binary operator`. Convert the text first: `as.numeric("5") + 1` is `6`.
variables.card.2: `paste("a", "b")` gives `"a b"`; `paste0()` joins without a space
variables-1.explain: `x` starts as 4. The second line stores `4 * 3`, which is 12, in `x`.
variables-2.explain: `paste0()` joins the three values without spaces. The number 4 becomes text.
variables-3.explain: `TRUE` and `FALSE` are `logical` values. R has no type called `boolean`.
variables-4.prompt: Which line stores the text Ana in the variable `name`?
variables-4.explain: `<-` assigns, and text needs quotes. Without quotes, R looks for a variable called `Ana`. `==` compares and does not store anything.
variables-5.explain: Numbers in R are `numeric` by default. Only `7L` is an `integer`.
variables-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] "HelloWorld"`.
variables-6.explain: `paste0()` joins the strings without a space. `paste()` would give `"Hello World"`.
variables-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] 43`.
variables-7.explain: `as.numeric()` turns the text `"42"` into the number 42, so `n + 1` is 43.
variables-8.prompt: Store the text Hi, followed by a space and the value of `name`, in `greeting`.
variables-8.explain: `paste()` puts a space between its values, and `<-` stores the result in `greeting`.
variables-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[1] 11`.
variables-9.explain: `x` must exist before `y` uses it. Then `y` is 10, and `x` becomes `10 + 1`.
variables-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
variables-10.pairs.0: stores a value in a variable
variables-11.explain: `"1"` is text, and you cannot add text to a number. Write `age <- age + 1`.
variables-12.explain: Names are case-sensitive. The variable is `city`, not `City`.
vectors.title: Vectors
vectors.summary: Keep many values in one vector, create sequences, pick elements by position and calculate with all elements at once.
vectors.lesson.0: A **vector** holds several values of the same type, in order. The function `c()` combines values into a vector. `print()` shows all elements on one line.
vectors.lesson.2: Now the `[1]` makes sense: a single value is a vector with one element. `length()` gives the number of elements of a vector.
vectors.lesson.5: `1:5` creates the whole numbers from 1 to 5. It also counts down: `10:7`. For other steps, use `seq()` with a start, an end and the step `by`.
vectors.lesson.7: Square brackets pick elements by position. R counts from 1, so `x[1]` is the first element. A vector of positions picks several elements, and a negative position removes that element.
vectors.lesson.9: `x[0]` is not the first element: it gives an empty vector. A position after the end, like `x[10]` for a vector of three elements, gives `NA`, which means "missing value".
vectors.lesson.11: Arithmetic works on every element at once: `prices * 2` doubles each price. Two vectors of the same length are combined element by element. `sum()`, `mean()`, `max()` and `min()` summarize a whole vector.
vectors.lesson.13: A vector has one type only. If you mix types, `c()` converts everything to one type: `c(1, "a")` becomes the character vector `"1" "a"`.
vectors.card.2: `x[1]` is the first element; `x[-1]` removes it
vectors-1.explain: R counts from 1, so `x[2]` is the second element.
vectors-3.explain: `seq()` starts at 2 and adds 3 each time while the value is not greater than 9: 2, 5, 8.
vectors-4.prompt: Which code gives the first element of the vector `x`?
vectors-4.explain: R counts from 1. `x[0]` gives an empty vector, `x[-1]` removes the first element, and `x(1)` calls a function.
vectors-5.statement: After this code, `y` contains the values `20` and `30`.
vectors-5.explain: A negative position removes that element, so `x[-1]` is everything except the first value.
vectors-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] 3`.
vectors-6.explain: `x` has three elements. `sum()` would give 12, `mean()` 4 and `max()` 6.
vectors-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] 3 4 5 6`.
vectors-7.explain: `3:6` counts from 3 to 6 in steps of 1. `6:3` would count down.
vectors-8.prompt: Create a vector with the numbers 1, 2 and 3 and store it in `nums`.
vectors-8.explain: `c()` combines the values into a vector, and `<-` stores it in `nums`.
vectors-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[1] 11 21 31`.
vectors-9.explain: First multiply every element by 10, then add 1. In the other order you get `20 30 40`.
vectors-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
vectors-11.prompt: The program should print the first score. Which line has the bug?
vectors-11.explain: R counts from 1, and `scores[0]` is empty. Write `scores[1]`.
vectors-12.explain: Parentheses alone do not create a vector. Write `x <- c(1, 2, 3)`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Compare values, run code only when a condition is TRUE with if and else, and test whole vectors with ifelse().
conditions.lesson.0: A **comparison** gives a logical value, `TRUE` or `FALSE`. `==` means equal (two equals signs), `!=` means not equal, and `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` compare sizes.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` runs code only when a condition is `TRUE`. The condition goes in parentheses, and the code goes in curly braces `{ }`. `else` adds code for the case `FALSE`. Write `else` on the same line as the closing brace: `} else {`.
conditions.lesson.4: `else if` checks another condition when the ones before it were `FALSE`. R checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch that matches.
conditions.lesson.6: If `else` starts a new line after the closing brace `}`, R thinks the `if` is already finished and stops with the error `unexpected 'else'`.
conditions.lesson.7: `&&` means **and**: both conditions must be `TRUE`. `||` means **or**: at least one must be `TRUE`. `!` means **not**: it turns `TRUE` into `FALSE` and the other way round.
conditions.lesson.10: A comparison with a vector compares every element and gives a logical vector. Inside square brackets, it keeps the elements where the result is `TRUE`. `&` and `|` combine logical vectors element by element. `ifelse(test, yes, no)` picks a value for every element.
conditions.lesson.12: Use `&&` and `||` in `if`, where you need exactly one `TRUE` or `FALSE`. Use `&` and `|` when you work with whole vectors.
conditions-1.explain: 12 divided by 2 leaves no remainder, so the condition is `TRUE`.
conditions-2.explain: `x > 3` is `FALSE` only for 2, so the brackets keep 4, 9 and 7.
conditions-3.explain: 85 is not at least 90, but it is at least 80. R runs only the first branch that matches.
conditions-4.prompt: Which operator means "not equal" in R?
conditions-4.explain: `!=` is not equal. The other operators do not exist in R.
conditions-5.explain: 3 is greater than 1 and less than 5, so both sides of `&&` are `TRUE`.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints adult when `age` is 18 or more.
conditions-6.explain: `>=` means greater than or equal. `>` is `FALSE` for exactly 18, and `=>` and `=<` are not R operators.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it labels every element.
conditions-7.explain: `ifelse()` works on a whole vector and picks `"high"` or `"low"` for each element.
conditions-8.prompt: Store the elements of `x` that are greater than 10 in `big`.
conditions-8.explain: `x > 10` gives `TRUE` or `FALSE` for every element, and the square brackets keep the `TRUE` ones.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints cold.
conditions-9.explain: `temp` must exist before the `if`. The condition is `TRUE`, so the first branch runs.
conditions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
conditions-11.explain: `else` must be on the same line as the closing brace. Write `} else {` and remove the `}` above it.
conditions-12.explain: `=` assigns a value. To compare, use two equals signs: `if (age == 20) {`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for and while, loop over positions with seq_along(), and learn when vectorized code is better.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop runs the same code once for every element of a vector. In `for (fruit in fruits)`, the variable `fruit` holds the next element in each round.
loops.lesson.2: A loop often builds a result step by step. Start with a value before the loop, then change it in every round. Here `total` starts at 0 and grows by each number.
loops.lesson.4: When you need the position of each element, loop over `seq_along(v)`. It gives the positions `1, 2, 3, ...` of `v`. It is safer than `1:length(v)`, because for an empty vector `1:length(v)` gives `1 0` and the loop runs anyway.
loops.lesson.6: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `TRUE`. Make sure that something in the loop changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.8: `break` stops a loop immediately. `next` skips the rest of the current round and continues with the next one.
loops.lesson.11: Many loops in R can be replaced by one vectorized expression. Both programs below double every price, but `prices * 2` is shorter and usually much faster. In the same way, `sum(x)` replaces a loop that adds up `x`.
loops.lesson.13: Use vectorized code when you do the same thing to every element. Use a loop when each step depends on the step before, like the `while` loop that doubles `n`.
loops.card.0: `for (x in v) { ... }` runs once for every element
loops.card.1: `for (i in seq_along(v))` loops over the positions
loops.card.3: `break` stops the loop, `next` skips a round
loops-1.explain: The loop adds 1, 2, 3 and 4 to `total`, which gives 10.
loops-2.explain: `n` goes from 100 to 10 and then to 1. Then `n > 1` is `FALSE`, after two rounds.
loops-3.prompt: How many lines does this print?
loops-3.explain: `next` skips the round with `i` equal to 3, so R prints 1, 2, 4 and 5.
loops-4.prompt: `v <- c(7, 8, 9)`. Which loop header gives `i` the positions 1, 2 and 3?
loops-4.explain: `seq_along(v)` gives the positions of `v`. `for (i in v)` gives the values 7, 8, 9, and `length(v)` is only the single number 3.
loops-5.statement: Both lines that print give the same result.
loops-5.explain: The loop adds every element of `x`, which is what `sum(x)` does in one step: both print `[1] 12`.
loops-6.explain: A `for` loop is written `for (variable in vector)`.
loops-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints only 1, 2 and 3.
loops-7.explain: `break` ends the loop when `i` is 4. `next` would only skip 4 and go on with 5. `continue` does not exist in R.
loops-8.prompt: Write the header of a loop that runs for `i` from 1 to 10.
loops-8.explain: `1:10` is the vector of whole numbers from 1 to 10, and `in` takes one element per round.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[1] 12`.
loops-9.explain: `total` must start at 0 before the loop. After the loop, R prints the sum once.
loops-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-10.pairs.1: repeats while a condition is TRUE
loops-11.prompt: The program should print 1, 2 and 3. Which line has the bug?
loops-11.explain: `n` gets smaller, so `n <= 3` stays `TRUE` and the loop never ends. Write `n <- n + 1`.
loops-12.explain: Round parentheses call a function. Use square brackets to pick an element: `words[i]`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with function(), pass arguments, give them default values and return results.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named piece of code that you can use again and again. You create one with `function()` and store it in a variable with `<-`. The names in the parentheses are the **arguments**: the values the function receives.
functions.lesson.2: A function gives back a **return value**: the value of the last line in its body. You can store it in a variable or use it in a calculation.
functions.lesson.4: `return(value)` leaves the function immediately and gives back `value`. This is useful when a function can stop early.
functions.lesson.7: Separate several arguments with commas. Write `= value` after an argument to give it a **default**: R uses it when the caller leaves the argument out. When you call a function, you can also name the arguments, like `by = 5` in `seq(0, 20, by = 5)`. Named arguments can come in any order.
functions.lesson.9: Inside `function()`, `=` sets a default. In a call, `=` names an argument. For normal variables, keep using `<-`.
functions.lesson.11: Because arithmetic works on whole vectors, many functions work on vectors without any extra code. The function below converts one temperature or a whole vector of temperatures.
functions.lesson.13: Variables that you create inside a function are **local**: they exist only while the function runs. After the call, R does not know them, and using them gives the error `object not found`.
functions.card.1: The last value is returned; `return(v)` leaves early
functions-1.explain: The inner call gives 10, and `double(10)` gives 20.
functions-2.explain: `area(4)` uses the default `h = 2` and gives 8. `area(1, 5)` gives 5. Together that is 13.
functions-3.explain: 10 is not greater than 10, so `return()` does not run and the function gives back the last value, `"small"`.
functions-4.prompt: Which line defines a function `add` that returns the sum of `a` and `b`?
functions-4.explain: In R you store the result of `function(arguments)` in a variable. The arguments always go in parentheses after `function`.
functions-5.explain: `total` is local to the function. After the call it does not exist, so `print(total)` stops with an error.
functions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] "Hi, friend"`.
functions-6.explain: The default value is the text `"friend"`, so it needs quotes. Without quotes, R looks for a variable called `friend`.
functions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it defines the function `half`.
functions-7.explain: R creates functions with the keyword `function`.
functions-8.prompt: Define a function `cube` that returns `x` to the power of 3.
functions-8.explain: `function(x)` takes one argument, and the last value in the braces, `x ^ 3`, is returned.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[1] 120`.
functions-9.explain: Inside the function, `tax` must be calculated before `price + tax` uses it. The last line calls the function after it is defined.
functions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
functions-10.pairs.0: creates a function with one argument
functions-10.pairs.1: leaves the function and gives back v
functions-11.explain: The function has no variable `y`. Divide by the length of the argument: `total / length(x)`.
functions-12.explain: The body starts with `{`, so it must end with `}`, not with `)`.
lists.title: Lists and apply
lists.summary: Group values of different types in a list, use names and $, and apply a function to every element with sapply() and lapply().
lists.lesson.0: A vector holds values of one type. A **list** can hold values of different types, even whole vectors. You create it with `list()`. Give each element a name with `name = value`, and get it back with `$` and the name.
lists.lesson.2: Double square brackets `[[ ]]` also get an element, by position or by name in quotes. `names()` gives the names of all elements, and `length()` gives the number of elements.
lists.lesson.4: To change an element, assign a new value with `$` and `<-`. If the name does not exist yet, R adds a new element to the list.
lists.lesson.6: Single brackets on a list, like `person[1]`, give a smaller list, not the element itself. Use `person[[1]]` or `person$name` to get the value.
lists.lesson.7: Applying a function to every element
lists.lesson.8: `sapply(x, f)` calls the function `f` once for every element of `x` and collects the results in a vector. Write the function name without parentheses: `sapply(x, mean)`, not `sapply(x, mean())`.
lists.lesson.10: You can also write a small function directly inside the call, like `function(n) n * 10`. `lapply()` works like `sapply()`, but it always gives back a list.
lists.lesson.12: For simple arithmetic, vectorized code like `nums * 10` is easier. `sapply()` is useful when each element is itself a vector, as in the list of scores.
lists.card.3: `sapply(x, f)` gives a vector, `lapply(x, f)` a list
lists-2.explain: `sapply()` calls `length()` for each of the three elements: 4, 2 and 1 values.
lists-3.explain: The list has two elements, `name` and `langs`. The vector inside `langs` counts as one element.
lists-4.prompt: You want the results as a list, even when every result is a single number. Which function do you use?
lists-4.explain: `lapply()` always gives back a list. `sapply()` simplifies the results to a vector when it can.
lists-5.statement: A list can hold a number, a string and a vector at the same time.
lists-5.explain: Unlike a vector, a list can mix types, for example `list(1, "a", c(2, 3))`.
lists-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] -3`.
lists-6.explain: `$` gets an element of a list by its name.
lists-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1]  3 12`.
lists-7.explain: `sapply()` calls `sum()` for each element and gives back a vector. `lapply()` would give back a list.
lists-8.prompt: Add an element `city` with the value Rome to the list `p`.
lists-8.explain: `$` with a new name and `<-` adds a new element to the list.
lists-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[1] 31`.
lists-9.explain: The list must exist first. Then `age` gets 30, and after that it grows by 1.
lists-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
lists-11.prompt: The program should print the name. Which line has the bug?
lists-11.explain: Names are case-sensitive. `p$Name` does not exist and gives `NULL`. Write `p$name`.
lists-12.explain: `sapply()` needs the function itself. Write `sum` without parentheses: `sapply(nums, sum)`.
dataframes.title: Data frames
dataframes.summary: Store tables in data frames, get columns with $, pick rows and columns with [ , ] and calculate with whole columns.
dataframes.lesson.0: A **data frame** is a table. Each column is a vector with a name, and all columns have the same length. You create one with `data.frame(column = vector, ...)`. `print()` shows the table with row numbers on the left.
dataframes.lesson.2: `nrow()` gives the number of rows, `ncol()` the number of columns, and `names()` the column names.
dataframes.lesson.4: `$` and the column name give you a column as a vector. Everything you know about vectors works on it, like `mean()` and `max()`.
dataframes.lesson.6: Square brackets with a comma pick rows and columns: `people[row, column]`. Leave one side empty to get all of it: `people[1, ]` is the whole first row, and `people[, "city"]` is the whole column `city`. You can use numbers or column names.
dataframes.lesson.8: A condition on a column gives `TRUE` or `FALSE` for every row. Put it before the comma to keep only the matching rows.
dataframes.lesson.10: To add a column, assign a vector to a new name with `$` and `<-`. Vectorized arithmetic calculates the new value for every row at once.
dataframes.lesson.12: Do not forget the comma. `people[2, ]` is the second row, but `people[2]` is the second column, as a small data frame.
dataframes-1.explain: Each column has three values, so the data frame has three rows.
dataframes-2.explain: `df$price` is the vector `2 6 10`. Its mean is 18 divided by 3, which is 6.
dataframes-3.explain: The condition keeps the rows with a price above 5, which are cup and bag, and `"item"` picks that column.
dataframes-4.prompt: Which code gives the second row of the data frame `df`?
dataframes-4.explain: The row comes before the comma. `df[, 2]` and `df[2]` give the second column, and `df$2` is not valid.
dataframes-5.explain: Row 1 of column `b` is the first value of `b`, which is 7.
dataframes-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] 3`.
dataframes-6.explain: The table has three rows. `ncol()` and `length()` both count the two columns.
dataframes-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `[1] "Ana"  "Cleo"`.
dataframes-7.explain: Inside the brackets you still need `df$` to get the column. `>=` keeps Ana, who is exactly 30.
dataframes-8.prompt: Add a column `final` to `df` that is `price` minus `discount`.
dataframes-8.explain: `df$final <-` creates the new column, and the subtraction runs for every row at once.
dataframes-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `[1] 2`.
dataframes-9.explain: The column `y` must exist before you filter on it. Two rows have a `y` above 15.
dataframes-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
dataframes-11.prompt: The program should print the average age, `32`. Which line has the bug?
dataframes-11.explain: `length()` of a data frame counts the columns, not the rows. Write `total / nrow(df)`.
dataframes-12.prompt: The program should print the first row. Which line has the bug?
dataframes-12.explain: Without a comma, `df[1]` is the first column. Write `df[1, ]` for the first row.
